newsitem.title: INDIA: India leaders gear for talks to avoid fresh polls.
newsitem.headline: India leaders gear for talks to avoid fresh polls.

text.p: India's political leaders prepared to hold talks on Saturday to avoid fresh elections after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's coalition fell following a defeat in a vote of confidence.
President Shankar Dayal Sharma accepted Deve Gowda's resignation on Friday and asked him to continue until arrangements were made to replace the 10-month-old centre-left United Front government.

But efforts to form a new government hinged on how the 15-party alliance could make a new bid for peace with its ally-turned-foe, the Congress party, which withdrew vital support to the government on March 30.
"We are prepared for any eventuality," Congress leader Sharad Pawar said. "The first chapter is over. We have to find out what the second part holds for us."
Both groups were scheduled to hold separate meetings to arrive at a fresh political formula. The United Front's decision-making Steering Committee was scheduled to meet at 8.30 a.m. (0300 GMT).
Their task looked tough, as Deve Gowda's caustic 75-minute reply at the end of a 12 1/2 hour debate on Friday deepened his differences with Congress president Sitaram Kesri.

Kesri accused Deve Gowda's government of not containing the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), against which the two groups made common cause last year after inconclusive elections threw up a fragmented parliament.
Deve Gowda said Kesri was an old man in a hurry to grab the country's top political job.
Last year, the United Front and Congress closed ranks to defeat a 12-day-old government led by the BJP, which emerged as the single largest grouping in parliament.
The centrist Congress and the United Front, which bands free-marketeers, regional groups and leftists, say the BJP favours India's Hindu majority and harms the interests of the Moslem minority.

In trying to arrange a government, President Sharma can invite the BJP again to form a new government, give the Congress party a chance or let a new arrangement work out between the Congress and United Front.
If all fails, elections would result.

After dropping his bombshell announcement on March 30, Kesri staked claim to the president for a Congress-led coalition, but later said the Congress would resume support to the United Front if it changed its leader.
The United Front has repeatedly rejected the demand, saying issues matter and not individuals.
But its leaders tossed up new names for leadership on Friday as the government headed for its ultimate collapse and prospects loomed large for a mid-term poll that most want to avoid.
Among the possible front-runners were G.K. Moopanar and Chandrababu Naidu, both regional leaders from southern India.

Opinion surveys show the BJP stands to gain from mid-term elections. The Congress and the United Front want to avoid a snap poll, but Deve Gowda said on Friday that he was ready to face the electorate.
"The final judgement...is before the nation of 950 million people," Deve Gowda said.
But he did not recommend to the president the dissolution of parliament, signalling a mood to prevent elections.
The numbers in the cumbersome parliament break-up do not easily add up to substantially favour any of the groups.
The United Front has 178 members, the Congress 140 and the BJP and its allies 193 in the 545-member lower house.
